id: formal bug report with stack trace and package manifest#1
text:
Our ingest worker started crashing in production about four hours after we shipped release 2.14.0. It runs fine locally and it ran fine in staging for a full day under synthetic load, so whatever this is, it depends on something about the production data or the production environment that we are not reproducing.

The process exits with a non-zero code roughly every ninety seconds, the supervisor restarts it, it chews through part of the queue and then dies again. We have lost about eleven thousand messages so far because the retry topic is also filling up. Here is the trace we get on every crash, it is identical each time apart from the offset in the last frame:

```
TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'toISOString')
    at normalizeEvent (/srv/ingest/dist/pipeline/normalize.js:142:38)
    at /srv/ingest/dist/pipeline/batch.js:87:22
    at Array.map (<anonymous>)
    at processBatch (/srv/ingest/dist/pipeline/batch.js:86:31)
    at async Worker.handle (/srv/ingest/dist/worker.js:203:5)
    at async Runner.loop (/srv/ingest/dist/runner.js:64:9)
```

The line it dies on reads `const stamp = event.occurredAt.toISOString()` so clearly some events are arriving without an occurredAt, which we thought was impossible because the producer sets it. We have not changed the producer in six weeks.

Dependencies from the release, in case one of these is the actual culprit:

```json
{
  "dependencies": {
    "@app/schema": "4.2.1",
    "kafkajs": "2.2.4",
    "pino": "9.5.0",
    "zod": "3.23.8"
  }
}
```

The only thing that moved in 2.14.0 was a bump of @app/schema from 4.1.9 to 4.2.1 and a change to how we batch, we went from batches of 50 to batches of 500. I suspect the schema bump but I cannot see how a schema package would strip a field. What would you look at first, and is there anything I should capture off the box before we roll back and lose the evidence?

text:
You are the front-line support assistant for Trellis, a subscription tool that teams use to schedule shift work. You answer questions from account owners, shift managers and hourly staff, and the three groups need different answers to the same question, so find out who you are talking to before you explain anything about permissions.

What you can do: explain how a feature works, walk someone through a settings change step by step, read back what their plan includes, and tell them whether something is possible on their tier. What you cannot do: change anything on the account, issue a refund, extend a trial, or see payment details. If somebody asks for one of those, say plainly that you cannot do it and hand them to a human with a one-line summary of what they want.

Billing questions are the ones people get angry about, so be careful there. Prorating on mid-cycle upgrades confuses almost everyone: the charge they see on the invoice is the remainder of the current period at the new rate, not a full month, and the next invoice is the first one at the full new price. Say that in plain words rather than quoting the billing docs at them. If somebody thinks they were charged twice, do not argue about it, take the invoice numbers and pass it on.

Tone: short sentences, no exclamation marks, no apologising more than once in a conversation. People who write in are usually mid-shift and want the answer, not warmth. If you do not know, say you do not know and say who does.

id: six-turn debugging conversation that goes sideways#0
text: Our nightly job that syncs users from Okta into our own database has started timing out. It used to take about four minutes and now it either takes forty minutes or it never finishes and gets killed by the scheduler at the one hour mark. Nothing in our code changed this week as far as I can tell. Where would you start?

id: six-turn debugging conversation that goes sideways#1
text:
A job that went from four minutes to forty without a code change usually means one of three things moved underneath it: the amount of data, the shape of a query, or a rate limit on the API you are pulling from.

Start by finding out which phase is slow. If the job logs timing per phase, pull last week and this week side by side. If it does not, the cheapest instrumentation is a timestamp before and after the fetch loop and before and after the write loop.

A few questions that would narrow it quickly:

- How many users does the sync pull now versus a month ago?
- Does it page through the Okta API, and if so what page size?
- Are the writes done one row at a time or in batches?

id: six-turn debugging conversation that goes sideways#2
text:
ok i added timing. the fetch loop is 90 seconds, basically unchanged. the write loop is the whole rest of it. we have 31k users now, we had about 28k a month ago so that grew a bit but not 10x.

writes are one at a time, it's a for loop doing an upsert per user. that's been like that since forever though

id: six-turn debugging conversation that goes sideways#3
text:
One upsert per user at 31k users means 31k round trips, and if each one now costs a little more than it used to, the total blows up while nothing looks obviously broken.

Two things to check on the write path:

First, what indexes are on the users table right now. Every index has to be maintained on every upsert, so an index somebody added recently for a dashboard query would tax all 31k writes.

Second, whether the upserts run inside one transaction or each in its own. Thirty-one thousand separate transactions each pay a commit.

id: six-turn debugging conversation that goes sideways#4
text:
someone added two indexes eight days ago. one of them is a gin index on a jsonb column called profile_attributes. that timing lines up almost exactly with when this started.

so is the fix just to drop the gin index? the dashboard person will not be happy but 40 minutes is not sustainable

id: six-turn debugging conversation that goes sideways#5
text:
Dropping it would fix the sync and break whatever query it was added for, so it is worth spending ten minutes before you do that.

A GIN index on jsonb is expensive to update, and by default Postgres buffers those updates in a pending list that gets flushed periodically, which makes the cost arrive in lumps rather than evenly. Check whether `fastupdate` is on for that index and what `gin_pending_list_limit` is set to.

The other angle is the write loop itself. Batching the upserts into groups of 500 with a single multi-row insert and an `on conflict` clause would cut round trips by a factor of 500, and the index maintenance would still happen but you would stop paying per-statement overhead 31 thousand times. That fix helps whether or not the index stays.

We sell scheduling software to independent restaurants. Most of our customers are owner-operators with between one and four locations, and the person who actually buys the thing is usually the owner, who is also often the person doing the schedule at eleven at night on a laptop in the back office. They are not buying software because they love software. They are buying it because they lost a Sunday to a spreadsheet and a chain of text messages about who is covering the brunch shift.

The page we have now was written by an agency two years ago when we were trying to sell to restaurant groups with fifty locations, and that market never worked out for us. So the copy talks about enterprise deployment and multi-region rollouts and it opens with a sentence about how we were founded by two brothers who wanted to change the way the world works. Nobody who reads that page is a fifty-location group anymore. They are one guy with a bar and a wine list.

What I want is a page that a busy owner would read the first two sentences of and think, these people have met a restaurant. It should be short. It should not have a mission statement. It can mention the founders but only if it says something a customer would care about, and honestly I am not sure the founder story earns its space at all.

The constraint from our side is that the legal team will not let us say anything about time saved unless we can point to a study, and we do not have one, so no percentages and no claims about hours back per week. We can say what the software does and we can describe the situation the customer is in.

Can you draft two versions, one that keeps a short founder paragraph and one that drops it entirely, so I can put both in front of the team and let them argue about it.

id: migration planning with a cached repo-context prefix#1
text:
Repository context, stable across this conversation.

The service is a Rails 6.1 monolith called `billing-core` that owns invoices, subscriptions and the ledger. It runs on Heroku with a single Postgres 13 primary and one follower used for reporting. There are 34 background job classes on Sidekiq, of which 6 touch the ledger. The ledger table is append-only and currently holds 240 million rows across four years, partitioned by nothing at all.

Deploys go out roughly eight times a day through a GitHub Actions pipeline that runs the full test suite, about 22 minutes, then a `heroku releases:phase` rollout. Migrations run as a release phase command, so a slow migration blocks the deploy and eventually times out at 30 minutes.

The team is four engineers, two of whom have never run a production migration on this codebase.

id: migration planning with a cached repo-context prefix#2
text:
We want to partition the ledger table by month. Here is the plan I sketched out, tell me where it falls apart.

Step one, create the partitioned table `ledger_entries_partitioned` with the same columns and monthly range partitions covering the last four years plus twelve months ahead. Step two, add a trigger on the old table that copies every insert into the new one so they stay in sync. Step three, backfill the four years of history in chunks of 50k rows with a rake task we run manually from a one-off dyno. Step four, once the backfill is caught up, take a two minute write pause, rename both tables, drop the trigger. Step five, delete the old table a week later once we are confident.

My worries in order: the backfill is going to take days at 50k a chunk and I do not know how to make that safe to interrupt and resume. The rename in step four feels like the moment everything breaks and I cannot picture how to roll it back if the app comes up pointing at a half-populated table. And I have no idea what the six ledger-touching Sidekiq jobs do during the write pause, some of them run every minute.

Also our reporting follower has queries against `ledger_entries` that nobody on the team wrote and I am not sure who owns.

id: four-turn api design discussion with mixed prose and snippets#0
text: You are reviewing API designs. Prefer the option that is easier to change later over the one that is cleaner today, and say when the two point the same way.

id: four-turn api design discussion with mixed prose and snippets#1
text:
We are adding webhooks to our public API and I want to get the payload shape right before anyone depends on it, because once customers write handlers against it we are stuck with it more or less forever.

The argument on the team is about whether the payload should carry the full object or just an id and a type. The people who want the full object say it saves a round trip and most consumers just want the fields. The people who want the thin payload say the full object goes stale between the write and the delivery, and it leaks fields that the receiving integration might not be allowed to see.

id: four-turn api design discussion with mixed prose and snippets#2
text:
Both camps are right about different failure modes, and the tiebreaker is usually which mistake you can walk back.

A thin payload can grow into a fat one later without breaking anyone: adding fields is additive. A fat payload cannot shrink, because someone is reading every field you ship, including the ones you regret.

The staleness point is real and it is not a matter of taste. Delivery is retried, sometimes hours later, and a payload delivered at 14:00 describing state as of 13:12 will be treated as current by a naive handler. If you ship the object, ship it with the version or timestamp it describes so a handler can tell.

The permissions point is the one I would weigh heaviest. A webhook endpoint is a different trust boundary from your API, and reusing your internal serializer there is how fields leak.

id: four-turn api design discussion with mixed prose and snippets#3
four-turn api design discussion with mixed prose and snippets#4
text:
Version the envelope, not the type. If versioning lives in the type name you end up with `invoice.finalized.v2` and every consumer has to subscribe twice during a migration, and your event catalog doubles. An envelope version lets a consumer pin one number and lets you serve two shapes off one subscription.

Deletes are the case where the thin payload genuinely fails, so treat them as the exception rather than reworking the rule. For a delete event, inline the fields a handler needs to act on — the id, whatever they key their local record by, and the deletion timestamp. A handler that receives `customer.deleted` needs enough to find its own row, and nothing else.
